newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares seen zooming after pro-market budget.
newsitem.headline: India shares seen zooming after pro-market budget.

text.p: Indian stock markets are expected to top smart gains on Saturday as bourses resume trade after the country's finance minister government presented a budget that traders described as "path-breaking" and "market-boosting."
"The markets should pretty much open with a bang and remain volatile," said Vikas Saraf, head of research at institutional brokerage SSKI Securities.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram who presented the 1997/98 (April-March) budget to Parliament late on Friday gave a pleasant surprise to the country's capital markets by fulfilling almost all expectations of traders and showed a strong commitment to the five-year old reform process.
"Over the next week, the market should move by about seven percent. There will be some renewed buying by foreign funds," SSKI's Saraf told Reutes.
The benchmark 30-share index of the premier Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) rallied 177.12 points, or 5.10 percent, to end at 3,651.91 in a day of wild swings.

"Brokers love the budget and they are just lapping up the shares, said Alok Sethi, director at Natwest Markets. So, clearly the market has taken a bullish stance overall and I would tend to go with it...."

Chidambaram announced a bold set of policy measures that met more than market hopes including sharp cuts in corporate and income taxes, allowing companies to buyback their shares and withdrawing a taxation on income from company dividends.
"I think the budget will give hope back to the country. This is an intellectually honest budget," said Ramesh Damani, a BSE member-broker.

The government also diluted a controversial minimum tax announced in the 1996/97 budget last year and raised the investment limit for foreign institutional investors in some firms to 30 percent from 24 percent

Business leaders were enthused by a plan to reduce the tax on domestic firms to 35 percent from 40 percent, and on foreign firms to 48 percent from 55 percent, the abolition of a tax on income from dividends and trimming of import duties.
"It is amazing how he has managed to unshackle 50 years of socialistic ideology. I give 10 plus to the FM," Damani said.
Market pundits had low expectations from a fractious 15-party centre-left goverment which had a tough task to kickstart a slowing economy, rejuvinate equity markets and cope with rising inflation.

Offsetting tax cuts, the budget would extend the tax net, currently limited to only about 12 million of India's 936 million citizens, by imposing new levies on owners of cars and telephones, and raising excise taxes on cigarettes.
"I think the bullish trend will continue for some time. Even the cats and dogs (penny stocks) should move up," RBalakrishnan, president at Dil Vikas Finance told Reuters.
"Multinationals are the biggest beneficiaries and will outperform the market. As they are among the higher tax paying firms, the tax breaks will help them."
Balakrishnan said he was bullish on the short-term market moveement.
"In this buying fever, it is quite possible that the index touches the 4,000 mark in the next week itself."
